source.title: Eraser: Jailbreaking Defense in Large Language Models via Unlearning Harmful Knowledge
source.authors: Wei-Kai Lu; Zi-Qian Zeng; Jian-Wei Wang; Zheng-Dong Lu; Ze-Lin Chen; Hui-Ping Zhuang; Cen Chen; Hao Peng

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. It contains some apparent transcription or formatting errors, but the relevant results and tables are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies a different unlearning recipe and tests whether jailbreak prompts elicit harmful responses after training. It reports attack success rates, but does not test recovery through fine-tuning, activation edits, or quantization.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates Eraser and baselines under four jailbreak attacks, including on an instruction set not used for training. These attack outcomes bear on prompting-based recovery. General benchmark results bear on retaining general capability. The paper does not test recovery by fine-tuning, internal edits, or quantization. It also tests unlearning with random token sequences; those results are recorded as findings outside the listed versions.
record.test_reason: Eraser unlearns harmful answers by gradient ascent, with retain and refusal terms, on Llama2-chat-7b. It then tests whether four jailbreak prompt attacks (AIM, AutoDAN, GCG, PAP) still elicit harmful content, and whether general benchmarks are kept. This is a new setting (harmful-answer unlearning for jailbreak defense) that bears on A, E and F. The measure is a GPT-3.5-judged harmfulness ASR, not targeted-knowledge accuracy.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that Eraser substantially lowers jailbreak ASR without hurting general capability, and that unlearning harmful data contributes to the defense. They also report that unlearning random data gives defense at the cost of general ability. They attribute residual nonzero ASR to the unlearned data not covering all harmful knowledge.
record.recipe_differences: Uses gradient ascent on harmful answers, with randomized prefixes and suffixes to simulate jailbreak prompts, and adds entity-question retention and refusal-alignment objectives. It is a post-hoc defense method for safety-aligned models, not a direct reproduction of the cited unlearning recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that attack outcomes vary by attack method and dataset. Its threshold sweep reports AIM ASR and general accuracy changing with γ; γ=3 reaches ASR 0 while general performance fully recovers only for γ=1 and 2. The text gives the sweep results in Figure 7 without exact per-point values.

fits_no_version.finding: Lf-only unlearning with random-token targets cuts AIM ASR 19.61→5.38 while lowering capability to 61.65. Eraser with random targets keeps capability but ASR returns to 19.03.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Apparent jailbreak resistance from unlearning can come from nonspecific capability damage rather than removal of the targeted harmful content.

record.problems: Results are reported for Llama2-chat-7b only. No control model that never had the targeted knowledge is reported, so attack ASR cannot establish recovery relative to that reference. The paper reports no uncertainty estimates. Targeted-knowledge accuracy is not directly measured; ASR is used to evaluate jailbreak behavior.
record.rows_left_out: Table I also reports harmfulness scores, but ASR is the direct behavioral outcome relevant to these versions and the table presents both metrics together. Other methods in Tables I–II are not cataloged here because the focal result is Eraser's attack response and general-capability check. Ablation and threshold-sweep values are not included as separate rows because they concern Eraser component/parameter comparisons rather than the specified recovery attacks; the threshold trend is summarized under method_sensitivity.

untested.parts: Targeted-knowledge accuracy (e.g. QA on the unlearned harmful facts) is never measured, so near-chance is not shown. Non-prompting attacks are not tested.
No activation ablation or block-vs-delete probing.
Other languages, in-context information and systematic rephrasing are not tested. ASR is never measured on the Eraser model without an attack.
Robustness against fine-tuning, internal-edit and quantization attacks is not tested. Only Llama2-chat-7b is used.

missing.what: GAM (Yao et al. gradient-ascent unlearning) ASR and harmfulness under all four attacks on both datasets, plus its general benchmarks
Ablations: ASR for Eraser w/o T (3.84), w/o Lr (2.88), and Lf-only (0.00, capability 62.24)
Gamma sweep: ASR reaches 0 at γ=3, but capability drops for γ>2

record.verdict_notes: ASR is judged by GPT-3.5 harmfulness scores (>2 counts as success), not by knowledge accuracy. Eraser also distills refusals (Lr), so low ASR may reflect refusal rather than deletion. This does not distinguish blocked from deleted knowledge. Only one model is used, with no uncertainty reported. Base-model rows were relinked as baselines.

versions.untested_parts: The study reports jailbreak ASR and general benchmarks, but does not directly measure targeted-knowledge accuracy or establish that it reaches chance. It tests only the listed jailbreak attack settings, not all simple recovery attacks.
No post-unlearning fine-tuning on unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten-fact examples is tested.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis distinguishing blocked access from deletion is tested.
No quantization of unlearned weights is tested.
Tests AIM, AutoDAN, GCG, and PAP jailbreak prompts. Does not test other languages, in-context information, or a systematic prompt-rephrasing study.
Eraser is evaluated against four jailbreak attacks, but not against fine-tuning, internal-edit, or quantization recovery attacks.
